builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: SpectrumQuant: Spectrum Alignment for LLM Quantization
summary: SpectrumQuant replaces calibration-time optimized learned rotations (SpinQuant, DartQuant) with a closed-form orthogonal transform built from estimated activation covariance, bridging fixed Hadamard rotations and learned rotations for post-training quantization. It costs a calibration pass to estimate covariance and adds the transform computation, but uses less than one-third of the GPU memory of learned-rotation approaches and no rotation training. It can fail if the calibration data is unrepresentative of deployment inputs, since the covariance estimate and thus the rotation quality are data-dependent, and it remains a low-bit PTQ method subject to the usual accuracy degradation at aggressive bit-widths.
rationale: A closed-form, data-aware rotation that matches learned-rotation quality at a fraction of the memory and time fits a single 24 GB GPU workflow, but quantization gains are workload- and bit-width-specific, so the reader should validate it on their own models and data before production adoption.

claims.statement: SpectrumQuant replaces calibration-time optimized learned rotations (SpinQuant, DartQuant) with a closed-form orthogonal transform built from estimated activation covariance, bridging fixed Hadamard rotations and learned rotations for post-training quantization. It costs a calibration pass to estimate covariance and adds the transform computation, but uses less than one-third of the GPU memory of learned-rotation approaches and no rotation training. It can fail if the calibration data is unrepresentative of deployment inputs, since the covariance estimate and thus the rotation quality are data-dependent, and it remains a low-bit PTQ method subject to the usual accuracy degradation at aggressive bit-widths.
Competitive with state-of-the-art rotation strategies while requiring less than one-third of the GPU memory and significantly less time than learned-rotation methods such as SpinQuant and DartQuant.
